chapters.title: PRELIMINARY RECKONING
paragraphs: These are the teachings of Master Sun.
For every nation, war is a matter of immense importance. The army determines whether people live or die: through it the State survives or is destroyed.
It therefore demands careful and sustained study.
In warfare, alongside strategy and circumstances, five things are essential. They are named, in order, The Way, Heaven, Earth, the Leader, and Law. None of these five can be left out.
The Way means right human conduct. When those who govern act honourably, the people stand together: they face danger without fear and place their lives at their Lord's disposal.
Heaven embraces Yin and Yang, cold and heat, the season and the time.
Earth concerns distance, character, size, and strategic location.
The Leader needs understanding, honesty, kindness, bravery, and firmness.
Law means dividing troops and arranging their organisation.
A commander must understand all these matters. Understanding them brings conquest; failing to understand them brings defeat.
We must also compare our situation with the enemy's, both in these respects and in the seven further matters that follow.
There are seven points to consider.

The ruler's moral character; the commander's competence; advantages supplied by nature; how disciplined the armies are; how strong the troops are; how well they are trained; and fairness in giving rewards and imposing penalties.
With this knowledge, I can predict who will win.
A commander serving me who follows my plans in battle wins consistently, and I keep him in my service. One who departs from those plans will lose and be removed from his command.

Thus, after considering these matters, finding the advantage on our side, and securing the generals' agreement, we establish circumstances that offer the prospect of victory. But neither the precise moment nor the method can be settled in advance: circumstances must shape changes to the plan.
Warfare involves pretence. When we are able to act, we present ourselves as unable; when we are close to our opponent, we suggest we are distant; when distant, we suggest we are close.

Tempt your opponent with a modest gain. Bewilder him and take him captive. Where you have shortcomings, present a faultless appearance and overawe him. Make a show of strength so that he stays away. Stir up his anger and disrupt his plans. Appear beneath him so that he looks down on you. If he has strength to spare, exhaust it; if his camp is united, divide it. Strike where he is vulnerable and turn up where you are least expected.
These are the successful planner's hidden methods. They must therefore remain undisclosed until the time for using them.

In the assessment made in the Sanctuary before battle, success belongs to whichever side surpasses the other in these matters. Those possessing many such advantages will win; those possessing few will fail to win; those possessing none are truly without hope.
Once I know how each side stands in these respects, I can predict which of them will win.

chapters.title: OPERATIONS OF WAR
paragraphs: Master Sun gave this teaching.

The needs of a campaign are these: one thousand light chariots, each drawn by four horses; one thousand chariots covered with leather; and one hundred thousand men in armour. Supplies must also travel to distant battlefields. Spending at home and on campaign, hospitality for guests, repair materials such as glue and lacquer, and everything needed to maintain armour and wagons together consume one thousand gold pieces every day. With that expenditure, an army of one hundred thousand can be assembled: the means of winning are then in your hands.
Yet even a successful campaign, if kept going too long, cools the troops' enthusiasm and wears down their weapons. If they undertake a siege, their strength drains away.

Moreover, a country cannot meet the demands of a war that continues too long. Once the troops are exhausted, their weapons dull, their power spent, and their money gone, neighbouring rulers rise against the weakened state. Even the wisest person cannot put matters right then.
Speedy completion has sometimes brought victory to an unskilled commander; but no skilled commander has ever profited by dragging out a campaign.
Indeed, no country has ever gained by keeping a war going for a long time.
Anyone who fails to understand the harm war causes will gain nothing from it. A capable campaigner needs no second recruitment of troops, nor a third loading of his supply wagons.
We bring weapons and military equipment from our own country, but can obtain enough food for the troops by taking it from our opponent.
The greatest burden on a state's resources is supplying troops on faraway battlefields. When the fighting is distant, its citizens are reduced to poverty.

Prices rise wherever an army is nearby, consuming the money of both troops and followers. The state's treasury also runs dry, requiring repeated levies. Military strength ebbs, money disappears, and the citizen's household is stripped bare: altogether, he loses seven tenths of his income. Public property suffers too: chariots break, horses wear out, and armour, helmets, arrows, bows, spears, shields, pikes, fighting towers, wagons, and oxen are consumed or lost. In this way, six tenths of the government's revenue is used up.

A discerning commander therefore tries to feed his men from enemy supplies. A single bale of their rice is worth twenty brought in our own wagons; one bundle of their animal fodder is worth more than twenty of ours.
Men must be given encouragement to defeat their opponent.
Reward those who secure an advantage over the opposing side.
Reward the first men to seize more than ten enemy chariots. Replace the enemy flags on those vehicles with ours, and put the captured vehicles into service alongside our own.
Treat the warriors who come with them kindly. In this way, as the opposing side suffers defeat, our own forces become stronger.
The purpose of warfare is to win, rather than to conduct protracted campaigns, however expertly they are managed.
A capable general holds the people's lives in his hands and watches over the well-being of the country.

chapters.title: THE ATTACK BY STRATAGEM
paragraphs: Master Sun gave this teaching.
The principles of warfare favour taking a country without a struggle over defeating it through burning and killing.
Taking the opposing army whole is preferable to beating it down after it has resisted fiercely.
It is preferable to take the "Lu," the "Tsu," or the "Wu" entire, rather than destroy these units on the battlefield.
Winning a hundred battles does not represent the highest achievement. The greatest skill lies in bringing an opponent into submission without resorting to combat.

The finest soldier therefore defeats his opponent's thinking with a better plan. Next comes the one who stops hostile forces from joining together; after him, the one who fights their army. Laying siege to their stronghold is the least desirable course.

Avoid a siege whenever there is any possible alternative. Before one can begin, three months must be spent building platforms, rams, and engines of siege. Another three months before the stronghold are then needed to construct the "Chuyin." The commander becomes angry and runs out of patience; his men swarm against the walls like ants before the proper moment, and one third die without achieving anything. These are the disasters that accompany sieges.

An expert in warfare therefore makes hostile troops submit without battle, takes their stronghold without a siege, and acquires their kingdom without a prolonged struggle. He secures the full benefit while his weapons remain untarnished.
This is what attacking through strategy means.

The rules of warfare prescribe encirclement when your strength is tenfold the enemy's, an attack when it is fivefold, and division when your numbers are double. With equal strength, fight with every effort. With fewer men, manoeuvre until an opening comes. If overwhelmingly inferior, give no opportunity for battle. Stubborn resistance by a smaller force only results in its being taken prisoner.
The soldier sustains the country. When his support is complete, the country must be strong; any shortcoming in that support leaves the country weak.
A ruler can hamper his own army in three different ways.
He may command the army on campaign to advance without realising that it should stay back, or order it to withdraw without realising that it should hold its ground.
This binds the troops as though they were tied with cord.
He may govern the troops just as he governs the state, despite knowing nothing of military business.
This leaves the men bewildered and uncertain.
He may determine where troops are placed without understanding the army's circumstances.
This plants suspicion in the minds of the troops.
When bewilderment and suspicion possess an army, neighbouring rulers become a threat. The troops are thrown into confusion and delivered into their opponent's hands.
Five circumstances allow us to predict a successful outcome.

The commander recognises when battle is appropriate and when it is not; he understands when many troops or only a few should be used; the people and their government agree; the state stands ready and attacks during an unguarded moment of its opponent; the commander is capable and his ruler leaves him free to act.
These five signs announce that success is coming.

An old teaching says that understanding both sides removes fear even through a hundred encounters. Someone who ignores his opponent and attends only to himself wins once and loses the next time. Someone ignorant both of his opponent and of the resources he himself possesses loses every time.

chapters.title: THE ORDER OF BATTLE
paragraphs: Master Sun gave this teaching.
The great commanders of old first put their own armies beyond defeat. Then they waited for their opponent to become vulnerable to certain defeat.
What brings defeat originates on our own side; what brings victory originates among our opponents.
Accomplished soldiers put defeat beyond possibility and also deprive their opponent of the ability to win.
Yet the written teaching warns that the circumstances needed to win may exist without always being available to us.
When winning is beyond reach, we defend our position; when success is assured, we go on the attack.
Shortage forces us to defend; abundance enables us to attack.
Expert defenders crouch concealed in the deepest darkness; expert attackers press onward to the very heights of heaven.
Follow these instructions, and the outcome will certainly be victory.

What ordinary people celebrate as a victory may not amount to real success. Winning a battle and hearing the kingdom declare, "You have done well," is not the highest achievement. Lifting an autumn fleece does not demonstrate strength. Eyes that can make out only the moon and sun have none of an eagle's keenness; hearing a thunderclap is no remarkable feat.

An old saying teaches that the accomplished soldier wins without desperate, blood-soaked encounters, and consequently gains no fame for cleverness or heroism. For him, entering battle means winning it: he attacks only after his opponent has already created the causes of his own defeat.
Furthermore, the capable soldier, secure in his own position, never allows the proper moment for attacking his opponent to slip away.
A successful army secures the conditions for winning before it goes looking for a fight.
An army headed for failure fights first, hoping that good fortune will make its weapons prevail.
The capable commander holds firmly to the "Way" and maintains the Law, thus directing the outcome himself.
The principles of warfare are said to proceed through five stages: the rule, the measure, the tables, the scales, and finally the prediction of success.

The rule surveys the territory; the measure establishes how much it produces; the tables record its inhabitants; the scales reveal their weight or quality. From this we can then work out whether the result will be success or failure.

On the scales, the army that will win outweighs the army that will lose as a beam outweighs a feather. When victorious troops attack, they resemble water long held back suddenly bursting down into deep valleys.
These are the arrangements that govern battle.

chapters.title: THE SPIRIT OF THE TROOPS
paragraphs: Master Sun gave this teaching.
Dividing a large body of men into smaller units makes it possible to command them just as one commands a small body.
Drums, bells, and flags make it possible to direct great numbers in combat in the same way that one directs a few.
An army is reliably protected from defeat by expertly alternating ordinary manoeuvres with extraordinary ones.
Understanding an opponent's strong and weak points, and using both reality and deception, allows us to crush him as a millstone crushes an egg beneath it.
In combat, moreover, the ordinary force engages the opponent, while the extraordinary force brings about his defeat.

Expertly directed, the extraordinary force endures like earth and heaven. It never stops, like rivers flowing and tides returning. It alternates endlessly like moon and sun, arriving and departing as the seasons do.

Five notes can be arranged into countless harmonies. Only five colours exist, yet blending them creates endless shades. Five tastes exist, yet combining them yields more flavours than our tongues can tell apart.

Warfare has only two forces, ordinary and extraordinary, yet their variations have no limit. They change into each other like a wheel revolving without a starting or finishing point. No one can fully unravel their mystery.
The troops' spirit resembles a rushing torrent carrying rocks along upon its shoulders.
Time the blow as precisely as a falcon judges its flight, striking and crushing its prey in an instant.
The effective fighter therefore has a terrifying spirit and strikes at sudden moments. He resembles a cocked crossbow: one touch of the trigger lets its taut string go.
Amid battle's bewildering noise and movement, confusion is absent; at the very heart of the fighting, the formation cannot be penetrated.
Complete discipline allows an appearance of disorder; real bravery allows an appearance of fear; genuine power allows an appearance of weakness.
Subdivision lets us imitate disorder; spirit lets us imitate fear; our fighting formation lets us imitate weakness.
By changing our formations, we compel our opponent to adjust to them, and so make him move.
Give the opponent an advantageous point and he is sure to seize it. By granting him that benefit, we draw him into motion and then descend upon him.

Thus the effective fighter looks to spirit for success, rather than relying wholly on his men's individual skill. He selects them carefully and entrusts the rest to the force of battle. Still, whenever an opening or advantage appears, he exploits it as far as it will go.
A log or stone rests motionless on level earth, but on a slope gathers force as it travels. Wait for your chance in that same way, and act with that force when the chance comes.
Under an accomplished general, the men's spirit has the momentum of a rounded stone sent rolling down from a lofty mountain peak.

chapters.title: EMPTINESS AND STRENGTH
paragraphs: Master Sun gave this teaching.
Arrive on the battlefield before your opponent and wait there for him: this preserves your strength.
Arriving behind time and rushing forward to encounter the opponent wears you out.
An effective fighter arranges for his opponent to come towards him. He refuses to let the opponent lure him in turn.
He offers something that looks profitable, drawing the opponent into a position that will defeat him. He sets obstacles in the way of any action that could endanger his own arrangements.
Disturb an opponent who rests in pleasant quarters. Deprive him of supplies if he lives in abundance. If he calmly sits waiting to be attacked, make him leave his position.
You can accomplish this by appearing where he is absent and striking at points he did not expect.
By travelling through places our opponent does not occupy, we can cover a thousand leagues without wearing ourselves out.
Positions left undefended by the opponent always fall when we assault them. In defence, however, we must be powerful even at points where an assault seems unlikely.
An expert attacker leaves the opponent uncertain about what needs defending; an expert defender leaves him uncertain about what can be attacked.

The hidden methods of attacking cannot be grasped as readily as a definite shape or a sound perceived by the senses. Once these methods have been learned, however, the opponent comes under our control.
Our attacks meet no effective resistance because they strike his shortcomings. Our withdrawals leave him unable to follow because we move away too swiftly.
Suppose we wish for battle, but the opponent rests content behind tall walls and broad, deep moats. We then strike at another place whose relief will force him to emerge.
When we wish to avoid a fight, we hold a line without fortifications and keep the opponent uncertain, thereby stopping him from attacking.
Feigned movements keep the opponent guessing about what we are doing. They allow us to concentrate while compelling him to spread out.
Our troops form a single body, while his are scattered into ten portions. Our united body strikes those divided ten. We are numerous where he is few, and that numerical advantage saves our strength.
Keep the intended point of assault concealed. Without knowing where the blow will land, the opponent has to prepare on all sides, leaving him weak at every point.
Reinforcing the front requires him to weaken the back. Reinforcing the right reduces strength on the left; reinforcing the left reduces strength on the right.
Preparing at every point means weakness at every point. The breadth of the opponent's preparations makes him weaker and makes us stronger.
Once we settle where and when to attack, we can defeat the opponent even though he is one hundred leagues distant.

Without knowing the terrain and the moment, the troops in front cannot aid those behind, nor the left aid the right, the right aid the left, or the rear aid the front. Parts of an army may be forty leagues apart; by comparison, four or five leagues is near at hand.
Wu has fewer troops than Yueh. But greater numbers do not necessarily ensure success, and so I maintain that victory can be ours.

If our opponent has many men, stop him exploiting that advantage and find out his campaign plan. Stir him into action to learn the condition of his troops; make a feint to test his position's strength. Spread and beat your wings to reveal whether his resources are adequate. Repeated feints and forays can make us seem impossible to grasp, an impression that neither spying nor cleverness can remove.

The commander shapes his plans around the opponent's arrangements and sets his armies moving. The mass of men cannot understand his purpose: they perceive the indications of success, but cannot work out how it is achieved.
Do not use a plan again merely because it once brought success. Change your methods as circumstances change.
An army can be compared with flowing water.
Water abandons the heights, leaving them dry, and runs into low places. Troops turn away from power and strike at what is empty.
The ground's contours direct the water's course. Acting to suit the opponent's condition is what brings military success.
Water has no predetermined shape; in the same way, the spirit governing warfare has no permanent form.
A commander who adapts his methods to his opponent and thus determines the outcome deserves the name God of war.
None of the five elements holds permanent precedence. The four seasons pass and return; days lengthen and shorten; the moon grows and diminishes. Warfare, too, has nothing permanently fixed.

chapters.title: BATTLE TACTICS
paragraphs: Master Sun gave this teaching.
Military business generally proceeds in the following manner.
The commander takes his ruler's instructions, gathers the troops, establishes harmony among them, and goes out on campaign.
Nothing is harder than battlefield tactics. The difficulty consists in reckoning distance and timing correctly and turning an unfavourable turn of events around.
A master of manoeuvre tempts his opponent with a gain that draws him onto a roundabout road, then sets out later yet reaches the destination ahead of him.
An army's actions can bring benefits; the quarrelling of an unruly crowd carries grave dangers.

If we use the entire army at once to gain an edge over our opponent, we may run out of time before achieving our aim. If only part presses ahead, the transport is lost. Suppose men throw aside armour and helmets, halt neither by night nor by day, cover twice the distance and perform twice the labour, then finally face the opponent one hundred leagues away. The result is the loss of their commander. The strongest arrive first while exhausted men fall behind, leaving only one tenth of the force ready for use.
A forced march of fifty leagues in pursuit of an advantage can bring failure to the advance guard's commander: only half of his troops will reach the destination.
Force an army to march thirty leagues for an advantage, and only two thirds of its men will be ready for use.
A shortage of ammunition, provisions, or other stores can also bring about catastrophe.
A ruler cannot negotiate with neighbouring rulers while remaining ignorant of what they intend.
A person unfamiliar with mountains, woods, narrow passes, and marshland cannot command an army on the march.
Without employing someone to guide him, a commander cannot turn the terrain to his benefit.
Conceal what you are doing; wait for a promising moment; separate or concentrate your forces as the situation requires.

Attack with the wind's speed; march with the forest's calm; lay waste like fire as you occupy. When defending, stand as solidly as a mountain, beyond the opponent's understanding like darkness. Move with the rapidity of a lightning flash.
Allow the greatest possible number to share in plundering, and divide among them the gains from the territory you seize.
Thus success goes to whoever understands both the winding route and the direct one.
These are the practices that make up battlefield tactics.

The old military writings explain that drums and bells serve where spoken commands cannot be heard, and flags help men to see. Bells, drums, banners, and flags bring all ears and eyes together in shared attention.
Once everyone acts together, brave men cannot press ahead on their own, nor can frightened men fall back without restraint. This is how a large body of men can be employed.
Accordingly, fighting at night makes extensive use of drums and signal fires, while fighting by day uses many flags and banners. These bewilder the opponent's hearing and sight.
In this way we intimidate his troops and frustrate the aims of their commander.

Men's spirits are eager in the morning, sluggish around noon, and inclined towards returning by evening. A commander who handles troops well therefore avoids the hour of their eagerness and strikes his opponent when his men are listless or turning towards camp.
This is how to put the changing character of energy to use.
Keeping your own heart governed means meeting disorder with discipline and noisy uproar with stillness.
Preserve strength by waiting for an opponent travelling from far away, meeting his hunger with your own fullness, and bringing fatigue against rest.
Where rows of flags flutter and tightly packed fighting ranks extend, withhold your attack and wait patiently for the right moment.
Avoid attacking anyone who occupies the heights or has heights behind him. Refuse to chase a pretended retreat, and do not assault troops whose spirit is high.
Refuse whatever bait the opponent puts before you.
Leave alone an opponent who has broken camp and is preparing to withdraw. When you encircle him, leave a way out. Do not bear down upon him when he is desperate.
These are the practices for putting soldiers to use.

chapters.title: THE NINE CHANGES
paragraphs: Master Sun gave this teaching.
Warfare generally begins in this fashion: the commander takes his ruler's instructions and then brings the armies together.

Avoid making camp in low or marshy places. Establish friendship with nearby states. Do not remain long in a distant land. Use cunning in wooded, mountainous terrain. When on death ground, give battle.

There are always some routes one must refuse to take, some troops one must refuse to assault, some castles one must refuse to besiege, some places one must refuse for battle, and some instructions from one's ruler one must refuse to carry out.
A commander familiar with the Nine Changes understands how soldiers should be used. Without that understanding, even his knowledge of the landscape cannot be put to work.
When directing armies, if you understand the practice of the Nine Changes, knowing the Five Advantages is of no use.
The discerning person weighs both benefits and drawbacks. He finds an escape from hardship, yet remains alert to danger even on the day he wins.
To bring an opponent into submission, do him every possible injury and draw him into pointless ventures. Tempt neighbouring rulers with profit as well, so that their actions follow your wishes.

In managing a campaign, therefore, trust your own readiness instead of assuming the opponent will stay away. Rather than assuming your stronghold will escape attack, ensure that every part is defended.
A commander must watch for five failings that place him in danger.
Thoughtless rashness carries him towards his death.
Excessive caution leaves him liable to be taken prisoner.
An easily roused temper exposes him to insult.
Excessive rigidity about proper behaviour opens him to dishonour.
Too much concern for the soldiers creates difficulties.
These five defects in a commander bring disaster in warfare. They cause armies to be overthrown and their leaders to be killed. They therefore demand close attention.

chapters.title: MOVEMENT OF TROOPS
paragraphs: Master Sun gave this teaching.
Consider the placing of troops and watching of opponents during warfare in the mountains.
Pass across mountains, then make camp in valleys, choosing secure positions.
Station your troops on elevated ground, and keep clear of an opponent occupying the heights.
Now consider operations near water.

Once across a body of water, move away from it at once. If an opponent is fording a stream, do not fight him in the water itself: strike after half his troops have crossed. Avoid advancing against an opponent beside water; instead, station your men securely on elevated ground.
Avoid battle if your opponent stands between your own troops and the river's source.
Now consider operations in marshland.
Move rapidly through salt marshes and avoid remaining in their vicinity.
If circumstances force you to fight near a marsh, find a position with grass and water, and plenty of trees at your back.
On open land, station the troops in a suitable position with higher ground behind them to the right. Death will then lie ahead, while safety lies behind.
This is the conduct of warfare on level land.
Following these practices enabled Huangti to defeat four Princes in war.
Troops generally favour the heights over low ground. They favour places reached by sunlight over those left in shade.
Care for the men's health and place their camp on elevated, sunlit ground: this will keep sickness away and ensure a successful outcome.
Where the land rises, make camp before the rise on its sunlit side. This benefits the men and allows us to make profitable use of the terrain.
If rain upstream makes a river surge, wait for its flow to settle before attempting a crossing.

Leave steep, impassable valleys quickly; likewise hollows like wells, cramped places, tangled ground that cannot be penetrated, marshes and bogs, and constricted passages containing traps. Do not go near them. Draw the opponent towards these places while remaining clear yourself. Face towards them, leaving them behind your opponent.
If cliffs, ponds, lakes, beds of reeds and rushes, or dense woodland lie near the troops, examine them completely. Such places are likely to conceal an opposing force waiting in ambush.
An opponent who stays quiet despite being nearby draws confidence from strong natural protection.
A challenge issued from far away is intended to make you come forward.
An opponent who makes his camp out in open country has a particular purpose for doing so.
Stirring in the trees indicates an approaching opponent. Treat broken boughs and flattened grass that suggest a great force has passed as grounds for suspicion.
Birds suddenly taking wing indicate a hidden ambush.
Frightened animals indicate that hostile troops are creeping closer from more than one direction.
Upright jets of dust rising high indicate the approach of chariots.
Broad stretches of dust hanging low indicate that foot soldiers are approaching.
Scattered narrow pillars of dust rising high indicate men gathering fuel for fires and fodder for animals.
Little dust clouds travelling back and forth indicate preparations by the opposing force to make a temporary camp.
Pleasant talk combined with energetic preparations indicates that the opposing force intends to move forward and attack.
Boastful language accompanied by horsemen being urged ahead indicates that the opposing force intends to pull back.
Light chariots moving up towards the sides of the camp indicate that the opposing force is coming out for battle.
A sudden request to suspend hostilities, made without discussion, points to a concealed purpose.
Messengers travelling back and forth, along with troops taking formation, indicate that the opposing force has a move in preparation.
Moving forward and then abruptly pulling back is meant to entice an assault.
When opposing troops lean on their weapons for support, they lack food.
When men sent to fetch water drink straight from the river, their army is thirsty.
Failure to pick up plunder that is within easy reach indicates that the troops are worn out.
Birds gathering around a position indicate that no troops are holding it.
Calls heard after dark indicate fear in the camp.
Confusion among the troops indicates that their commander is not being heeded.
Shifts in the placement of standards and flags indicate unrest among the troops.
Officers become angry when their men are exhausted and respond slowly to commands.
Slaughtering horses to eat indicates that the opposing force is running short of food.
Cooking vessels suspended on the wall, with the men no longer turning in, indicate that the opposing force has exhausted its resources.
Overly warm and familiar behaviour by a commander indicates that his men no longer have confidence in him.
Rewards given again and again indicate the collapse of discipline.
Repeated penalties indicate that the commander finds himself in trouble.
A commander who starts by bullying and then becomes servile lacks understanding of the situation.
Anyone who presents apologies along with hostages is eager to obtain a truce.
If two forces keen to fight remain facing one another for a long while without moving forward or back, the situation calls for the greatest alertness and care.
A large number of men does not guarantee power.
Even troops unable to mount a rushing assault may win, provided they act together and have learned their opponent's condition.
Someone who dismisses his opponent without first thinking carefully is certain to become a prisoner.
When a commander unfamiliar to the troops punishes them, they stop following his orders. Troops who will not obey cannot be put to effective use.
Troops who know their commander but remain unmoved by the penalties he imposes are of no use either.
Kind treatment secures compliance; authority secures consistency. Together these bring us success in war.
People taught to obey from the outset give due respect to the instructions of their commander.
People who have not been taught obedience early fail to give their commander's instructions due respect.
Where commander and men understand one another, instructions are consistently carried out.
